In a recent development, for TVs that support 4K, the Streaming Stick Plus is a step up, offering sharper resolution and support for HDR10 and HDR10+ while keeping the same compact, USB-powered design as the HD model. According to recent reports, for anyone looking to improve their TV's sound along with its streaming capabilities, the Roku Streambar SE combines both in a single device and is currently $89, down from $149.99. It supports 4K streaming with HDR10 and HDR10+ and uses two 1.9-inch full-range drivers with a bass port to deliver fuller audio than most built-in TV speakers.

  • When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research.
  • Every Christmas, we turn to the same stories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature. Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026. Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is presently in the process of writing.

Every Christmas, we turn to the same stories. The same movies the grandparents like, and the song that plays every single Christmas Eve so that everyone in the family can sing along. It is comforting to have stories to return to. Many of the traditions we return to were actually cemented by none other than Charles Dickens. A Christmas Carol is the most popular, having been adapted hundreds of times. Dickens cemented Christmas as we know it today, but that doesn't mean there aren't other Christmas stories worth knowing.

In a recent development, A Christmas story can be a Christmas story for many reasons. The setting, for instance, sets the mood, but the values are what stay. During this time of year, it is normal to gravitate toward stories with deeper meaning that reflect on what one is grateful for. Some books have achieved this with incredible mastery. Here are the best.

Sources indicate that "'Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents,' grumbled Jo, lying on the rug." Louisa May Alcott's Little Women might not be everyone's go-to Christmas story, but it should be. The word "Christmas" appears twice in the first sentence of the book and, within the first couple chapters, the March sisters have already given away their Christmas breakfast to a hungry family. It is something out of a Dickens story.

Sources indicate that the original Little Women volume, not including its continuations, takes place over a year, bookended by two very different Christmases. During this time, Alcott subtly shows the importance of maintaining the values we so cherish during the festive season year-round. Marmee often encourages her daughters to be selfless, humble, studious, and caring. By the end of this volume, Beth is recovering from scarlet fever and the sisters receive the best present they could have wished for: their father's return. The book is perfect for the holiday season.

In a recent development, claire Keegan's novella Small Things like These is quietly heartbreaking. Set in Ireland in 1985, it follows Bill Furlong, a coal and fuel merchant. The week before Christmas, he goes about his routine while thinking about what presents to get his wife and daughters. One day, he visits a local convent and is surprised to find a young woman named Sarah locked in a nearby shed and asking about a baby. He frees her and leaves her with the Mother Superior, who says she was playing a game. The girl reminds Bill of his mother, who was an unmarried teenager when she got pregnant with him. Over the following days, Bill cannot shake the suspicion that something terrible is going on in the convent.

It has been revealed that this story shows that Christmas stories do not need to be wrapped in a pretty bow. It is also possible to read something themed to the season that deals with ethical questions. In the case of Small Things like These, Keegan discusses the difficult topic of Ireland's Magdalene laundries, where young women were imprisoned and forced to do labor. The subject is treated with the dignity and care it deserves, showing how a single person can choose to do what is right in the face of larger injustices, even when the cost is high.

Recent findings suggest that hogfather is missing. The Auditors of Reality, a group of celestial bureaucrats, have hired the assassin Mr. Teatime to murder Discworld’s Santa Claus equivalent, who gives children presents on the night of Hogswatch, on December 32nd. Without children's belief in Hogfather, the sun won't rise. The only one who understands the importance of Hogfather's role is Death, and so he must step in. Aided by Albert, his reluctant pixie servant, Death puts on a red suit and starts delivering presents. His granddaughter, Susan, is tasked with traveling to the Tooth Fairy's realm to bring Hogfather back.

As funny and magical as all of Terry Pratchett's stories, Hogfather is a wonderful seasonal read. In addition to an incredible display of whimsy, the book includes one of the most thoughtful discussions of the importance of faith and why we go to such great lengths to keep the magic of the holidays alive. "Humans need fantasy to be human," Death tells Susan. "To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape.".

According to recent reports, after Dickens, Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky has a monopoly on Christmas. However, not many people know that the Nutcracker ballet, often performed during the holiday season, is based on Alexandre Dumas' story, which is itself an adaptation of an older (and much darker) short story: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King by E. T. A. Hoffmann.

It has been revealed that one Christmas Eve (of course), Marie notices a nutcracker under the tree. That evening, while playing with the nutcracker, she sees mice start to come out from beneath the floor. Their leader seems to be a seven-headed Mouse King, taller than all the others. Suddenly, all of Marie's toys come to life and, led by the nutcracker, begin to fight the mouse army. They are at a disadvantage, so Marie throws her slipper at the Mouse King to stop him from capturing the nutcracker. The morning after, Marie wakes up with a bandaged arm and no idea if the events she witnessed were real. The only person who believes her is her godfather, who then tells her the tragic story of Princess Pirlipat and Madam Mouserinks, the Queen of the Mice, which explains the origins of nutcrackers.

Yes, this story was written by the same author who wrote both Breakfast at Tiffany's and In Cold Blood. And yes, it is a perfect Christmas classic. Truman Capote's "A Christmas Memory" is set in rural Alabama in the 1930s. It was inspired by Capote's own life and his experience of the holiday season in a family with financial difficulties. The short story is beautiful, warm, funny, and deep. It will also absolutely break your heart.

“It's fruitcake weather!” Buddy's elderly cousin reveals, declaring the start of winter. The relationship between the seven-year-old boy and his cousin is the heart of Capote's story. They are two childlike, wide-eyed people in a stern and strict family. During the story, they gather the ingredients to make fruitcakes and share them with friends. Years later, Buddy looks back at the simple magic of those shared Christmases. The prose is as beautiful as the story, and it is worth reading, if only for the last few lines. The cousin character is mentioned to have been inspired by Sook, a relative the author lived with as a boy, who may have had intellectual disabilities. Capote called her "a genius.".

Sources indicate that the plot of this story is as simple as most people's holiday celebrations. Dubliner Gabriel Conroy is a teacher and part-time book reviewer. One winter evening, he attends a party with his wife, Gretta, hosted by family members. There is music, pudding, a goose, and tipsy guests. While greeting friends and old acquaintances, Gabriel thinks of the speech he has to give. At the end of the evening, a guest sings a sorrowful song. Gretta is moved by the song, and later confesses it reminds her of a young man she once loved who has passed away. Gabriel could be anyone. What makes him stand out is the beautifully crafted way he thinks about life and death.

Industry observers note that "The Dead" closes James Joyce's Dubliners. At almost 16,000 words, it can also be a short novella. Whatever its definition, the story is timeless and deeply moving. It discusses local topics related to Irishness, while reflecting on universal themes such as love and loss. The ending, "His soul swooned slowly as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling, like the descent of their last end, upon all the living and the dead," might be one of the most beautiful and poignant lines in the history of literature.

Sources indicate that what is a 14th-century Middle English chivalric romance doing in a list of Christmas books? Well, it is a great story, and it is set at Christmastime, so it meets every requirement to be here. A warning: it is written in alliterative verse, so it might be denser than other picks, although J. R. R. Tolkien himself has an accessible translation. Still, it is absolutely worth the effort. And what better way to end the year's reading challenge than with a classic?

Recent findings suggest that sir Gawain and the Green Knight takes place in King Arthur's court during the celebrations between Christmas and Fresh Year. Suddenly, a giant green knight interrupts the feast. He offers his axe to any man who dares to strike him. However, in return, that person will agree to take a blow in a year and a day. Sir Gawain, one of King Arthur's knights, accepts and beheads him. A year later, on the way to that appointment, Gawain is taken in by a generous lord and his wife. What follows is a game of temptation and a test of honor that Gawain must pass.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

Say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Sources indicate that swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

Sources indicate that A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

Sources indicate that the update follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Sources indicate that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In a recent development, in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn rapidly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Recent findings suggest that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

According to recent reports, he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

It has been revealed that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

Recent findings suggest that on the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Sources indicate that space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

It has been revealed that the European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

Recent findings suggest that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Industry observers note that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

Industry observers note that the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

It has been revealed that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

It has been revealed that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Industry observers note that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Industry observers note that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

Recent findings suggest that if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller states with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

Recent findings suggest that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” states Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

It has been revealed that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

It has been revealed that the countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Recent findings suggest that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

It has been revealed that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

Industry observers note that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” notes Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Recent findings suggest that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Recent findings suggest that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as promptly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

In a recent development, “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller claims. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

It has been revealed that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Ridley Scott’s 116-Minute Sci-Fi Masterpiece 'Alien' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Netflix

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you need any convincing as to why Ridley Scott is held in such high regard by movie fans, you only need to fire up Netflix before November 30 and catch his classic Alien.
  • Set in the year 2122, the film takes place in a future where galactic space travel is not only possible, it’s industrialized.
  • Scott conceived of the idea after the success of Star Wars, bringing his own brand of intensity to deep space and making a star of Weaver, who was appearing in her first starring role and just her third movie appearance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you need any convincing as to why Ridley Scott is held in such high regard by movie fans, you only need to fire up Netflix before November 30 and catch his classic Alien. The pioneering sci-fi horror movie led to a franchise consisting of seven films, two spin-offs, and the TV hit Alien: Earth. However, back in 1979, it was just Scott’s vision that terrified audiences and changed the genre as we know it, with star Sigourney Weaver becoming an icon for the ages. If you’ve never experienced the nail-biting first chapter of the space saga, now is the time.

Set in the year 2122, the film takes place in a future where galactic space travel is not only possible, it’s industrialized. Commercial towing craft Nostromo is diverted to a planetoid, answering a distress signal from an alien spacecraft. Once there, an alien attaches itself to one of the crew without his knowledge, only to burst out of him once he's back on board. Escaping to the dark corridors of the ship, the alien (known as a Xenomorph) grows rapidly and starts hunting down the crew members one by one. Only Ellen Ripley (Weaver), who had reservations about the diversion in the first place, stands a chance of outwitting this terrifying new foe.

Scott conceived of the idea after the success of Star Wars, bringing his own brand of intensity to deep space and making a star of Weaver, who was appearing in her first starring role and just her third movie appearance. Nearly 50 years after its release, it’s still considered a pivotal moment in the sci-fi genre and film in general, thanks to the risks it took with well-known formulas.

Sources indicate that prior to Scott’s film, the idea of space travel was mostly aspirational for Hollywood studios. Star Trek invited us to “boldly go where no man has gone before,” Star Wars offered swashbuckling adventures, and a decade on from the Apollo 11 moon landing, space seemed like a frontier. What Alien did was introduce the idea of space as a void, a lonely stretch of isolation where its inhabitants were alone in the truest sense. Scott took that concept and used it as the basis for a classic “haunted house” horror tale, teasing theater patrons with the poster’s tagline: “In space, no one can hear you scream.”.

It also broke barriers with its visual presentation. The alien creatures and environments designed by the Swiss artist H. R. Giger looked otherworldly, inspired by surrealistic landscapes and biomechanical concepts. The spaces surrounding Ripley were foreign and unsettling, adding to the sense of being alone against this creature that has no empathy or reason, only the instinct to kill. Its influence is immeasurable – if you’ve seen a sci-fi movie where the crew of a spaceship are picked off by a deadly stowaway, it’s likely Alien’s DNA is in there. In the gaming world, titles like Halo and Doom both share the themes of the movie and its sequels. Its most impactful element, however, was its human star.

It has been revealed that ellen Ripley would have been an outlier in science fiction simply for being a female lead, but her influence goes beyond simple box ticking. She wasn’t like the cavalier heroes we were used to seeing flying through asteroid fields or battling little green men. In Alien, she is pragmatic, resourceful, and tough, doing what she has to do to survive without flourishes or grandstanding. She remained the key component of the first four Alien movies, and inspired a number of female sci-fi lead characters in the years since. The gritty resilience of The Terminator’s Sarah Connor, the relentlessness of Katniss Everdeen, and the strength of Mad Max hero Furiosa all owe something to Ellen Ripley, making her a key component of centering female characters in a historically male-dominated genre.

Given her influence on women in genre filmmaking, it’s surprising that the character was originally written as male, with no dialogue changing when the gender was flipped. Speaking to the American Film Institute in 2009, Weaver pointed out this as what attracted her to the part. “It was a character written as a man, so it was written in a very straightforward way,” she said. “She’s a direct person, who didn’t suddenly have these scenes where she was vulnerable. She didn’t throw up her hands and wait for someone to save her.”.

Ridley Scott's Alien still holds up nearly half a century later, providing a benchmark by which all follow-ups, and sci-fi in general, are compared. The simplicity of the storytelling, combined with the complexity of the visual filmmaking, made for an unforgettable deep space nightmare that left everyone wondering what horrors may lie just beyond the stars.Alien is on Netflix, with November 30 as the final day to watch.

According to recent reports, apple doesn’t offer a timeline on when CarPlay Ultra will actually be available through any other brand beyond Aston Martin. The company also does not have a dedicated list of automakers that have signed on to support CarPlay Ultra listed on its website.

According to recent reports, when Apple declared the next-generation version of CarPlay at WWDC 2022, however, it stated that several brands had committed to supporting the platform. In May of last year, Apple touted that three new partners had signed on: Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis.

However, several brands have also dropped their aims to support CarPlay Ultra. Mercedes-Benz was originally on Apple’s list, but abandoned its plans to support next-generation CarPlay in 2024. According to the Financial Times, Audi, Volvo, Polestar, and Renault have also decided against supporting CarPlay Ultra, despite originally being touted as partners by Apple.

With all of that remarked, here is the full list of automakers who strategy to eventually support CarPlay Ultra, as of November 2026.

What do we know beyond this list? Not a whole lot. Interestingly, Top Gear reported that the Hyundai IONIQ 3 EV would support CarPlay Ultra. Hyundai confirmed the IONIQ 3 in April, but has not commented on whether the vehicle will support CarPlay Ultra as rumors suggested.

Mark Gurman at Bloomberg has also reported CarPlay Ultra will launch for “least one major new Hyundai/Kia model in the second half of this year.”.

While Apple has touted Ford as a partner for CarPlay Ultra, the automaker recently signaled it’s not too impressed with the first version of a platform.

In a recent interview, Ford CEO Jim Farley was asked whether the organization is “considering” CarPlay Ultra support. Here’s what he said:.

In a recent development, “We are. We don’t like the execution in round 1 of Ultra, but we’re very committed to Apple. I’ve talked to Tim many times about this.”.

It’s better than a flat “no,” but perhaps not the enthusiasm Ford drivers might have hoped to hear.

The question at this point is whether any other automakers have ditched CarPlay Ultra. Ideally, Apple will provide a full list sooner rather than later, but in the meantime, this is the only information we have.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

Aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

Want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross indicates the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

Tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—right now only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

Sources indicate that controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

What are your top Apple Home accessory recommendations? Let us know in the comments.

#142886. Tech Report: The Perfect ‘Hunger Games’ Cast if the Movie Were Made in 2026

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3376 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Perfect ‘Hunger Games’ Cast if the Movie Were Made in 2026

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pop culture found its favorite love triangle when The Hunger Games was transformed into a blockbuster movie franchise.
  • With the highly anticipated The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reigniting the obsession with the original, it’s time to ponder what The Hunger Games might look like if it were made in 2026.
  • The Hunger Games lives and dies with Katniss Everdeen, the Girl on Fire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pop culture found its favorite love triangle when The Hunger Games was transformed into a blockbuster movie franchise. Based on the young adult novels by Suzanne Collins, the filmis set in a dystopian future in the nation of Panem and follows a teenage girl named Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised, annual fight to the death. Alongside her fellow district tribute Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), she must survive the brutal arena while unintentionally sparking a rebellion against the oppressive Capitol.

With the highly anticipated The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reigniting the obsession with the original, it’s time to ponder what The Hunger Games might look like if it were made in 2026. In our dream iteration, we will fill the ensemble with rising generational stars alongside legends of the craft while reflecting the nature of the characters both in the book and on screen. Though the original cast may be untouchable to some devoted fans, this list is what dreams are made of.

The Hunger Games lives and dies with Katniss Everdeen, the Girl on Fire. Tough and fiercely protective, Katniss sets the action in motion in the first film when she volunteers as tribute after her sister Primrose's (Willow Shields) name is drawn at the reaping for the 74th Hunger Games. Armed with exceptional archery skills, a sharp survival instinct, and a guarded demeanor, she enters the arena alongside fellow District 12 tribute Peeta Mellark. After her breakout Oscar-nominated role in Winter's Bone, The Hunger Games proved that Jennifer Lawrence could play a stoic, self-reliant young woman forced into a gritty, mature environment. Lawrence brought natural athleticism, quiet wariness, and ferocity without over-glamorizing the story's brutal elements.

It has been revealed that lawrence masterfully balanced a relatable authenticity with grounded maturity. She was a reluctant, real-world survivor who was never pretentious, carrying the high-stakes dystopian thriller by projecting real fear and compassion. One young star who masters everything that elevated Lawrence's Katniss is Sadie Sink. Showcasing her knack for portraying complex teenage heroines, Sink excels at playing a guarded young woman who conceals deep trauma and fierce loyalty beneath a tough exterior. Between Max Mayfield in Stranger Things and her recent turn as Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day, Sink is no stranger to massive franchises and is never intimidated. While the character would embark on a romantic love triangle, Sink's iteration of Katniss would be fiercely independent and self-reliant. Her ability to play raw, authentic dramatic parts, as seen on Broadway in John Proctor Is the Villain and in the film adaptation of The Whale, would add gravitas, rooting Katniss in weighted reality.

Recent findings suggest that hailing from District 12, it's Peeta Mellark. The lovelorn baker's son has harbored a long-standing crush on Katniss, so, of course, it added intrigue for viewers watching the 74th Hunger Games, as Peeta and Katniss had a star-crossed lovers' narrative built around them. Unlike other hardened competitors, Peeta used verbal skills, artistic camouflage abilities, and genuine empathy to survive. Joining Katniss in defying the Capitol's orders, Peeta emerged as a co-winner and helped spark the revolution that followed. The green-flag boy of the story, Josh Hutcherson brought authentic emotional depth and warmth to the role, making it easy to champion him. With a gentle spirit and sincerity, Hutcherson instilled a protective love and strategic charm into Peeta that was rightly earned.

Recent findings suggest that peeta served as the emotional core of The Hunger Games. To take on this part today, an actor who has the will to battle without diminishing his genuine heart and spirit is required. That actor is rising superstar Walker Scobell. Best known for starring in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell would be a compelling Peeta due to his charm, sarcastic wit, and ability to balance vulnerability with fierce loyalty. Oh, and he's well-versed in action-centric storytelling. Scobell is naturally earnest and charming, which would seamlessly translate to the character. His smile is instantly disarming, though how much smile is there really when you're inside the arena? Though Scobell is a teen action hero, Peeta is defined more by his deep empathy, artistic heart, and emotional resilience. As seen in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell balances those traits through a pure tenderness. Energetic and expressive, there's a universe in which Scobell would be even more beloved than Hutcherson, and that's quite a high bar to achieve.

It has been revealed that young adult stories need a tinge of a love triangle, and in The Hunger Games, Gale Hawthorne filled that third slot. He is Katniss' best friend and hunting partner, and they share a similar hardscrabble life. Gale fiercely hates the Capitol and the oppressive system of the Games, questioning why anyone would watch them. He serves as the emotional support for Katniss' family while she's in the Games. In the film, Gale was played by a hunk: Liam Hemsworth. He naturally captured Gale's quiet intensity, physical stature, and silent protectiveness. His expressive presence was a means of communication. It also served as a stark contrast in stature to Hutcherson's Peeta.

Industry observers note that hemsworth balanced the range of emotion necessary to bring Gale to life. Playing Gale requires conveying deep loyalty, heartbreak, and quiet resolve against his underlying rage and revolutionary spark. Rather than leaning closer to a Hollywood heartthrob or Gale's physical likeness in the book, the perfect pick would be David Iacono. Tall and muscular with olive skin, dark hair, and gray eyes, Iacono fits the classic look of District 12's "Seam" neighborhood. Audiences are quite familiar with Iacono's ability to play a devoted, caring romantic interest during his time as Cam Cameron in The Summer I Turned Pretty. He excels at portraying the quiet tenderness that Gale would share with Katniss in the woods before the Games tear their lives apart. Recent findings suggest that with the upcoming film fleshing out the full lore and mythology of Haymitch Abernathy, it will only deepen the allure of this fascinating character. It has been revealed that and now we begin our adventure into the colorful world of eccentric individuals! First up, the utterly fabulous Effie Trinket. Evil was personified in the form of President Coriolanus Snow. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

This post is sponsored by PITAKA.

Industry observers note that plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

According to recent reports, most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:.

It has been revealed that if you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Industry observers note that spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

According to recent reports, if you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:.

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

In a recent development, the iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

Industry observers note that the iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Industry observers note that apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for owners who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

#142876. Tech Report: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2970 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.
  • Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.
  • Recent findings suggest that last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Recent findings suggest that last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully debuted on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

According to recent reports, this mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

Recent findings suggest that “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” notes Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”.

Industry observers note that phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX released on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA.

In a recent development, MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

It has been revealed that if all goes according to plan, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images.

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” notes Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” says Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

In a recent development, from that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot.

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

Industry observers note that the best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

Industry observers note that before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu indicates, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA.

In a recent development, it will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Sources indicate that idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR.

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

It has been revealed that A simulation highlights how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR.

Sources indicate that once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” claims Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

Sources indicate that the WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she notes. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”.

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR.

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday notes.

According to recent reports, despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday notes Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy.

According to recent reports, idefix’s interactions with its newly introduced home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec states. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”.

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel states the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

Industry observers note that once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

The MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel notes. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”.

According to recent reports, probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA.

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA.

According to recent reports, during the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA.

In a recent development, finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel notes. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu notes. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) introduced earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

According to recent reports, with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

Sources indicate that when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company states this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

Sources indicate that I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the newly introduced speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that customers are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

It has been revealed that have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.
