‘Hejira’ at 50: Beck, Cameron Crowe, Clairo, and More Honor Joni Mitchell’s 1976 Masterpiece

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that J oni Mitchell wanted to go ice skating.
  • Sources indicate that mitchell had recently cancelled the remainder of her Hissing of Summer Lawns tour, performing her last show at the nearby Dane County Memorial Coliseum.
  • Legendary photographer Joel Bernstein captured this moment, which would eventually appear inside the gatefold for her next album: Hejira.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that J oni Mitchell wanted to go ice skating. It was February 1976, and she was standing on the edge of a frozen Lake Mendota in Madison, Wisconsin, wearing a black ermine cape and a black wool hat. All she needed were black skates to match. “I had a hell of a time getting the guy to give me black skates,” she recalled to Cameron Crowe, decades later. “He said, ‘Black skates are for, for men, madam.’ I said, ’No, no, you don’t understand. I’m having a funeral for my dead tour. I need black.”.

Sources indicate that mitchell had recently cancelled the remainder of her Hissing of Summer Lawns tour, performing her last show at the nearby Dane County Memorial Coliseum. She was exhausted, battling a cocaine addiction, and reeling from the breakup with her drummer John Guerin, which she’d later describe as “one of the most special relationships” she’d ever had. This was her wake for it all, a farewell ride through the ice — not so different from the “River” she dreamt about skating on just five years prior. The ice was starting to thaw, and there were loud crashing sounds coming from the nearby trees, a sound she likened to “cases of Coca-Cola smashing.” She began to skate anyway, her black outfit standing in stark contrast to the backdrop.

Legendary photographer Joel Bernstein captured this moment, which would eventually appear inside the gatefold for her next album: Hejira. On the front cover, taken by Norman Seef, she’s wearing a black beret and holding a cigarette, stoically staring at the camera (she wanted it to look like an Ingmar Bergman film, she stated), as a wide, open road is juxtaposed below. The artwork indicated the mission statement of Hejira — in the same way she skated away on that ice and didn’t look back, Mitchell got in her car and drove. “The Hejira album was written mostly while I was traveling in the car,” she told Crowe, in her 1979 Rolling Stone cover story. “That’s why there were no piano songs, if you remember. Hejira was an obscure word, but it said exactly what I wanted. Running away, honorably.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Mitchell took three journeys while making Hejira: a portion of Bob Dylan’s all-star Rolling Thunder Revue Tour in late 1975, her short-lived Hissing trek in early 1976, and a cross-country drive she made in a white Mercedes without a license (she’d often wear a red wig in disguise, and go by names like Charlene Latimer and Joan Black). Released in November 1976, the album is a timeless travelogue of jazz-folk magic, when Mitchell left it all behind in search for more. “I’m porous with travel fever,” she sings on the aching title track. “But you know I’m so glad to be on my own.”.

Sources indicate that it’s impossible to pinpoint the genius of Hejira on just one track. There’s the opener “Coyote,” about the affair she had with the playwright Sam Shephard on the Rolling Thunder tour. That song is now immortalized in a viral video from Martin Scorsese’s documentary, where she casually performs it for a stunned Dylan, Roger McGuinn, and Gordon Lightfoot. There’s “Furry Sings the Blues,” about her encounter with the Memphis blues legend who didn’t exactly take a liking to her (yes, that’s her longtime pal Neil Young on the harmonica). The stunning “Amelia,” named after Amelia Earhart, was her ode “from one solo pilot to another …sort of reflecting on the cost of being a woman and having something you must do.” Hejira is arguably her most cohesive body of work, featuring the fretless bass of Jaco Pastorius — whom she called the bass player of her dreams — plus guitarist Larry Carlton, percussionist Bobbye Hall, and others.

Looking back, Mitchell knew she was at the height of her powers. “I feel a lot of people could have written ’Chelsea Morning,’” she remarked. “But I don’t think anyone else could have written the songs on Hejira.” In honor of the 50th anniversary of Hejira, Rolling Stone spoke with musicians and actors about its legacy, and why it continues to resonate with listeners today. And in a full-circle moment, Crowe, who is presently working on a Mitchell biopic, pays tribute to the record he discussed with Mitchell in this very magazine, all those years ago. Related Content Clairo Covers Beloved MF Doom Song With El Michels Affair 'Grief Is Universal — And Very Specific': Diana Silvers on Her Devastatingly Beautiful New Record See Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis Spoof 'You Can See Everything' Beck Regrets Turning Down ‘Zoolander’ Character That Went to David Bowie.

I’ve been a Joni Mitchell fan for a really long time, since I was a kid. And one of my best friends who passed away, we were obsessed with her. She was the one who actually introduced me to Joni Mitchell through Blue, because we would just listen to the album all the time. So through a general obsession with her, I just eventually went through all of her albums. And I really remember being particularly attached to Hejira when I was a teenager. I would go on long walks around my neighborhood [in Oak Park in Illinois], listening to that album, and just be really emotional.

It has been revealed that jaco’s bass literally captures the feeling of being on a trip and moving. He uses his bass as a vehicle on that album in such a cool way. And Joni’s lyrics feel like being on a road trip, listening to somebody’s stories. It reminds me of being with my parents, driving. We always drive from Chicago to Georgia where my family’s from, and just being on the road and talking.

Industry observers note that the album itself feels like a departure. She’s going on a journey and choosing to go away from the industry for a minute, and that is captured sonically in a really interesting way. With Hejira, she distills the feeling of loneliness in a way that she hadn’t done before. Each song is dealing with loneliness, but she puts it into these different scenarios and narratives. They all come together to tell this one story of being a woman who’s alone, just traveling.

It has been revealed that in Martin Scorsese’s film The Rolling Thunder Review: A Bob Dylan Story, there is a moment where Joni plays her newly introduced song, “Coyote,” at Gordon Lightfoot’s house. I love that there is footage of the early creation of this song. The lyrics change a little on the album, but you can see in her eyes the memories are very powerful as she sings and remembers. She had just written “Coyote” on a bus when she was with the tour, as she looked out at the “white lines on the freeway,” after she had a brief, tumultuous affair with the playwright Sam Shepard. Most of us have had these youthful, quick assignations, and I love being in her head as she reconciles the moment through her poetry and lyricism. Hejira is filled with emotion and hunger and as a young woman. Hejira helped me with the complexities of life, love, and longing.

Industry observers note that it’s something that stayed with me my whole life. Being somebody who makes records and always having trouble listening to records because you’re just always thinking about technically how they were made, it’s a beautiful example of just being so disconnected from any kind of process. It doesn’t bear examination. I just find it 100 percent an emotional reactive experience. It conjures up something that I am so desperate to hold onto in my life. Basically what I’m saying is, I’m just a sad, pathetic fan, really.

Those things get chipped away gradually, as you meet all your heroes and make a lot of music. You never really listen to music the same way. But I’m a teenager again when I listen to it. I don’t know if it’s the imagery or the fact that she has this incredible way of weaving a narrative that is just so difficult to do in song. I mean, poetry is powerful, but the combination of melody and poetry is this kind of witchcraft that has always cast a spell on me.

She’s my favorite artist. And this record is an apex of confidence. She’s really just doing what she wants, to the nth degree. She’s this crazy sort of enigmatic, weird figure. You hear all these stories about her. She’s a manifestation of something that is so rare and special that my version of her that I have in my heart and my idea of who she is, I’m just clinging onto it for dear life. It’s like a hero I never want to meet. She could be the nicest, warmest person on Earth, but she wouldn’t be this person that she’s created in my mind personally, by my personal relationship with her music.

According to recent reports, I remember hearing a long time ago that Joni wrote most of Hejira while she was on a road trip across America, and ever since then, I’ve always listened to it on long drives. It just makes so much sense to me. The whole record feels like it’s constantly moving, whether you’re speeding down a highway or sitting in traffic watching the sun go down.

As a drummer first, I’m always listening for the drums and percussion on records. To me, they’re kind of the heartbeat of any modern album. I know a lot of Joni’s records don’t have much drumming on them, but the fact that Hejira is constantly chugging along without a lot of full kit drumming continues to blow my mind. And I think Jaco’s bass playing adds this whole other rhythmic dimension to her music.

I’ve always thought of Joni as a percussionist in her own way. The way she attacks the guitar strings, the rhythms she creates with her strumming, it’s unlike anything I’ve ever heard from another musician. It’s one of the most fascinating things about her playing to me. And then you have Jaco on bass, another absolute master of rhythm, and the two of them create this incredible, almost hypnotic pulse that runs through the whole record.

Industry observers note that and Bobbye Hall’s percussion adds so much to that feeling. It’s never overpowering, but there’s so much movement and texture in what she’s doing. All these little rhythmic details that somehow make the music feel even more alive. Between the three of them, there’s this constant sense of motion, like the music is always pushing forward but never in a hurry to get anywhere.

Hejira was the Joni album that helped me meet Joni. I feel like her truest self comes through on this record so beautifully, and it’s an anchor on tour when the roads are never ending and the bus forever rumbling. My favorite song is “Coyote.”.

Sources indicate that hejira is Joni’s culmination to my mind. Her greatest songs, the greatest band, the greatest recordings, the most revelatory. The signature Roland Jazz Chorus guitar amp tone. Jaco Pastorius truly unleashed. The concepts and material mined into their seventh and eighth minute in some cases. I like to believe her whole catalog was leading to this moment. She’s at the height of her powers, and the masterworks that follow (Don Juan’s Reckless Daughter, Mingus, Night Ride Home, Turbulent Indigo, etc.) feel possible because of what Hejira unlocked. The writing is perhaps the most challenging, but the experience remains incredibly propulsive; you’re carried along by bearing witness to a human truly unrestrained by self-doubt, by adhering to any kind of rules or any kind of culture, someone in the midst of their quest to express their purest self. Maybe that sounds vague, but anyone that knows the record knows exactly what I’m talking about. When I’ve been asked about it, I’ve jokingly replied, “It’s as far as music has come.” But maybe that’s actually true.

I was touring extensively through my twenties, and I think it was at least 10 months of the year I was just on the road constantly. It was such a grind, but music had become a companion. We all had our headphones, and you’d sit on these long plane rides and bus rides listening to records. So it’s a lot of time to take a lot of deep dives. The whole Odelay tour, I was listening to Joni on the bus. It was pretty much Joni, Françoise Hardy records from the mid Sixties, and Morricone soundtracks — but not the Westerns, the weirder stuff. And then I had a CD of a rainstorm in Hawaii. That was all I listened to. It was like Joni and a Hawaiian rainstorm.

Sources indicate that hejira is the sound of an artist who has evolved so deeply into their own voice and their own craft. It’s a thing to behold. It’s a place that not a lot of artists even get to. Either they’re not really on that search to cultivate that rarefied place in their work, or they’re distracted by success and fame and touring, which happens to anybody who gets caught up in the sort of mechanics of the music business. So I think it’s even more of a singular achievement that she was able to make this after being on such a nonstop, relentless decade of making albums and touring. Usually at that point, somebody would just want to disappear for five years.

In a recent development, the music doesn’t necessarily sound like anything she had done before. One thing that’s really striking to me is the guitar sound. The effect on her guitar is a chorus pedal. The first one came out the year she was making the record. This was brand newly introduced technology. So this is like, “This new weird thing came out, and I’m going to put it on my entire album.” Not even, “Let’s vet this and see if this is cool. Is this going to be trendy? Is this going to sound dated?” This chorus pedal becomes the sound of whole genres afterwards. I don’t think it really becomes part of the palette of popular music till maybe the early 2010s. You listen to almost all of indie rock, from Mac DeMarco, to pop artists.

Recent findings suggest that and then you also get the guitar sound of Prince’s Purple Rain, which comes from this record, without a doubt. It is interesting that something that is uncompromising, and not even her most popular album or most iconic, still managed to have an imprint on pop. Honestly, I think the sound of this even filters into shoegaze and Cocteau Twins. I don’t know if people have put those things together, but I see it clearly.

She is so mature as an artist on this record. I mean, it would take you more than a lifetime to get to that maturity. Somehow, she did it.

Recent findings suggest that I first listened to Hejira in full on a tour bus driving through Europe. Highway rushing past, barren fields and long stretches of countryside out the window, the way Joni intended (I think). It struck me immediately as a timeless record. None of the songs are shorter than four minutes, the longest one being almost nine, but somehow they all feel intentional. She doesn’t waste words. I was so intrigued by that concept, of letting the story speak for itself, and setting up a bed of guitars that could support it. It inspired my writing a lot during that time, specifically a song I wrote while on that tour called “Our Strange Ways.” This record feels hypnotic and deeply meditative. And listening to it as I felt, quite literally, like a prisoner of the white lines on the freeway, was an experience I will never forget. One of my top Joni records of all time.

Long country drives are still my favorite way to pass the time, and Hejira captures why better than any other record I’ve heard. There was a year maybe where I’d point the car in some direction and only play Hejira, on a loop, until I’d memorized every melodic variation and phrase, as if getting a handle on the twists and turns of those infinite songs would give me a better handle on the twists and turns of life itself. I love the interior drama, the humor, the mise en scène, the acceptance of uncertainty and change. The chords, the tunings, obviously. My dad idolized Jaco growing up and makes his own fretless basses, so I hear my dad playing with Joni on the Jaco songs.

Recent findings suggest that once when I was making lectures for a songwriting class I was undeservingly teaching, I tried writing one about, forgive me, the “multi-perspectival sublime.” I wanted to relate Hejira to the painting “Las Meninas” by Velázquez and how, the longer you look at both, the harder it is to make sense of you-the-viewer’s place in it. Looking at “Las Meninas,” at first the viewer feels that everyone in the painting is looking baldly at them, but as you look closer, you realize the “viewer” is in an impossible position, and likely isn’t in the room at all. The songs on Hejira do this for me. They seem to be about the self, but the perspective shifts rapidly, from a man and a woman sitting on a rock to a blue motel room to a marble bowling ball, from a roadside gas station to the cosmos, a chimney becomes a flag reflected from a bank window into a hotel room — the center is always shifting, to such a degree that the viewer loses their sense of self and surrenders to liminality in a sort of holy way.

I didn’t finish the essay because it’s hard to write about a feeling like that without reducing it to platitudes, and I’m no Peter Schjeldahl. But Hejira really does help me transcend the self, with its trick mirrors and micro-to-macro shifts and its sense of spiritual surrender and leggerezza. It’s my deepest musical attachment, no question.

Recent findings suggest that god, this record. I had a dream once where Joni was sitting on a dock on a lake in Canada singing “Coyote,” with all my family in the water, singing along in the sun. Needless to say, this record and Joni’s voice has been extremely influential to me, even making its way into my dreams!

In a recent development, the freedom in this record, the six-, seven-, eight-minute long songs, her storytelling, taking you on the long and winding road with her. She always reminds me there are no rules. I think my favorite song is “Amelia”: “It was the hexagram of the heavens/It was the strings of my guitar.” She is the master. I am so grateful to have been introduced to Joni so young, her voice as a North Star.

Sources indicate that something I love and admire about Joni is that she never made the same record twice, even though she easily could have, considering how strong her lyrics are on their own. I love the way Joni uses the electric guitar on Hejira. To me, it sounds like rain running down the window of a moving car, which feels so fitting when you think of the record as a kind of travel diary.

I remember the first time I heard “Amelia.” I kept thinking, how does she write a song about someone or something so far removed from my own life, and yet make me see so much of myself in it? Or the way she uses the Cold War as a metaphor in “Blue Motel Room.” That’s what Joni’s lyrics do. They hold a mirror up to whoever is listening without ever seeming to try too hard. Something I often ask myself when I’m writing, especially when listening to a song like “Blue Motel Room,” is how to bring the wider world into the microcosm of everyday life. How do you take something so vast and make it feel so intimate? Joni does that beautifully, and I think it really shines through on Hejira.

Joni Mitchell is one of those songwriters that I go to whenever I have writer’s block — she always provides a well of inspiration. My song “Keep You” is a direct homage to “Coyote” that evoked a scandalous song about love through a free spirit. Lines like “you’ll be brushing out a brood mare’s tail” were scrubbed into imagery like “brushing out the mane of a silver healer.” I love to pull from Joni’s work. She is a huge inspiration to me.

It has been revealed that I don’t even know where to begin with Hejira, because it has touched my life in so many profound ways. At first, when I was little and just old enough to hum along to the melodies. Again, when I was a few years older and learning how to play “Coyote” on the guitar. And then a few years later, when I started reading the lyrics of songs I liked and being inspired to start writing my own, which led to my career in songwriting. I remember driving from Maine to L.A. in pursuit of my dream, during which I, of course, listened to Hejira, because I felt as though I was living every lyric in real time. Now as a 34-year-old woman, I continue to return to it as if it’s a friend going through all the same growing pains I’m going through — constantly in search of something, and simultaneously asking if the big dream is worth the loneliness that often comes with it. Even though it’s nearly impossible to choose a favorite song from the record because they are all so intertwined to me, if I had to pick, I’d say “Amelia.” Everything about it. The chord changes. The guitar tones. And of course the perfectly poetic yet heart-wrenchingly clear lyrics that describe two women choosing ambition, exploration, and the unknown. I’m forever grateful to Joni for this album, and my life would be drastically different without it.

Industry observers note that hejira lives in its own world, a sonic-travelogue written on Mitchell’s 1976 journey across America. It’s her most cinematic album too, filled with restless wonder and the characters she’d met along the way. The album was born out of the end of Mitchell’s relationship with drummer John Guerin. They’d lived and toured together. “We had a hard time letting each other go,” says Mitchell today. Her popularity was at a peak after Court and Spark, but a tour of America’s arenas left her missing the intimacy and sound of smaller venues and clubs. She cancelled an upcoming European tour, went skating on Madison, Wisconsin’s icy Lake Mendota (the “bird in flight” series was memorably captured by photographer Joel Bernstein) and headed back to California with the notion that it was time to travel, soak up life, seek new inspiration, and find a course-correction before she became “another scribe writing about the life of a rock singer, a minority experience to be sure.”.

In a recent development, life soon arrived with an invitation. Mitchell’s old friend from Toronto, Australian race-champion Vic Wilson, visited Mitchell with his flight-attendant friend Steven. Wilson was looking to borrow a car for a road-trip to Damariscotta, Maine, where he planned to collect his daughter, Larissa, and return to Australia. Mitchell not only loaned them the Bluebird, her white Mercedes coupe, but enthusiastically joined them with guitar, a suitcase, and sketchpads. (Her car would soon break down and need to be replaced on the road.) Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Marry at Palm Springs Wedding.

Sources indicate that parting manufacturer with her road-trip buddies in Newly introduced York city, Mitchell rode back alone. It was America’s Bicentennial summer. With roadmaps (and no driver’s license), she worked her way down the East Coast, through Charleston, South Carolina, the pageantry of small town parades, pinball buddies, flag-draped cafes. Though the disguise rarely escaped close examination, Mitchell often wore a red wig and traveled by the name Charlene Latimer. At night she collected the thoughts of the day and wrote songs filled with longing and delight and raw introspection. “I knew it was a growth step for me,” she reflects today, listening to “Song For Sharon” and other songs from the album. She adds one small disappointment. Nearly back home from her solo return, Mitchell stopped to join Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder revue for a show in Ft. Worth. Her artist’s portfolio containing all the Hejira drawings were stolen from her hotel room.

The songs remain. Each one is filled with memory and detail and stunning reflection, but don’t forget to listen to Hejira as a whole. There’s a movie in every full-listen. To further appreciate Hejira, it’s also fun to consider what popular music sounded like in the summer of 1976. It was the peak of disco, radio was filled with the Bee Gees, the thump-thump-thump of post-Saturday Night Fever. Heard in context today, especially with the bass explorations of Jaco Pastorious, Hejira sounds like music from another planet. For any fan who joined the Joni Mitchell journey with Blue, the elixir of Hejira is the adventure you didn’t expect. Mitchell’s own rules for writing the album: “Summon a melody and some chords, write the words …then ask yourself if you’ve done anything like it before. If you have, start over.”.

#142786. An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Chrhenning

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so.
  • Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.
  • Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.

Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.

Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.

Sources indicate that in my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis .

Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes indicates how plausible each one is, given what we know.

It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty:.

The line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure.

It has been revealed that A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters.

It has been revealed that all of these need the uncertainty to be useful. To see when it is, it makes sense to look at where it comes from.

As a running example, we look at steering angle prediction. The input is the image from a car’s front camera, and the output $y$ is the steering angle. Such datasets can be recorded cheaply from human drivers. Take a car approaching a point where the road splits. In the left lane, drivers mostly go left. In the right lane, they mostly go right. In the middle lane, which points straight at the divider, about half go left and half go right.

The car’s position across the lanes is implicit in the camera image. To keep the figures simple, we use it directly as a one-dimensional input $x$ in the figures below.The rest of the image, such as where the road goes, matters just as much for the prediction. We implicitly assume that the model knows it, since it cannot be compressed into a simple one-dimensional variable that keeps the explanations easy to follow.

Sources indicate that what we want to learn is the conditional distribution $p^*(y \mid x)$: for each position, how likely each steering angle is. As is common in statistical learning theory, we assume that the data come from a fixed joint distribution $p^*(x, y)$, and the recordings from human drivers are samples from it.

Recent findings suggest that the ground truth $p^*(y \mid x)$ is just one of many possible conditional distributions.Strictly speaking, the truth is only defined where $p^*(x) > 0$. Many hypotheses agree with it on the road but differ off the road, where no data can tell them apart. We call each conditional distribution of $y$ given $x$ a hypothesis, and together they form a space. As we will see, learning amounts to searching a subset of this space.

It has been revealed that that subset is the model, a family of hypotheses indexed by parameters $\theta$. A common choice for regression is a Gaussian whose mean is a neural network $f_\theta(x)$ and whose variance $\sigma^2$ is fixed:.

The truth need not lie inside the model. For the lane split, it does not: a single Gaussian has one peak, but in the middle lane the truth has two.

In a recent development, training picks the hypothesis that best explains the data. It minimizes the negative log-likelihood (NLL), the average of $-\log p_\theta(y_i \mid x_i)$ over the training examples. For the Gaussian with fixed variance, this is the familiar mean squared errorI walked through this connection, from the KL divergence to the mean squared error, in an earlier post.:.

So a network trained with mean squared error already has an uncertainty model, even if nobody chose it on purpose.

How far is the trained model from the truth? The expected NLL splits into two terms:.

where both expectations are over the true data distribution. The first term is the KL divergence, which measures how far the model is from the truth and is zero only if they match. The second is the entropy of the truth, its aleatoric uncertainty, which does not depend on the model. Minimizing the NLL therefore moves the model toward the truth. But we never know the entropy of the truth, so the NLL alone cannot tell us how far away we still are.This is why we are usually blind to model misspecification: a low NLL does not tell us whether the truth lies inside the model. I will get back to this later. Moreover, even the KL divergence would not be enough, since it is an average over all inputs. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so a model can be close to the truth on average and still steer into the divider. Knowing which inputs matter takes domain expertise, which is ultimately the modeller's responsibility.

Back in the middle lane, the single peak has a dangerous consequence. The mean squared error is minimized by the average steering angle, and the average of left and right is straight ahead, into the divider. No choice of parameters avoids this, because every hypothesis in the model has a single peak. In an earlier post, I looked at this example in more detail, and we studied it in a paper on misspecification, the case where the truth lies outside the model .

In a recent development, the fix is a model that contains the truth. For this example, a mixture of two Gaussians, whose weights, means and variances are all outputs of the network, is enough to contain the truth.

Understanding the problem well enough to make this choice is the modeller’s job. But a richer model is not free: it contains more hypotheses, so the data has to do more work to single out the right one.This is the familiar bias–variance tradeoff. For example, a fully connected network can represent everything a convolutional network can. Yet for images we use convolutional networks, because they leave out hypotheses that do not fit images and so need much less data. Their assumptions seem stronger than necessary, though: with enough data, vision transformers, which assume less, do better.

Recent findings suggest that since the mixture contains the truth, enough data brings it close, including in the middle lane. Only then is its spread the aleatoric uncertainty: with the given information, even a perfect model cannot say which lane a particular driver will take.As with the coin flip, what counts as aleatoric depends on what the input contains. If $x$ were random noise, it would carry no information, and the best fit would ignore it and learn the distribution of steering angles independent of the input, $p(y)$. A rear camera image is more deceptive. Steering changes slowly (it is strongly autocorrelated), so the view behind the car indicates how the driver steered a moment ago, and repeating that is usually a good guess. The validation error decreases as expected during training, yet the model can never anticipate a turn, because the road ahead is not in the input. I discuss this gap between predicting and forecasting in an earlier post.

But in practice we do not know the truth, so we cannot check the fit like this. How do we know how much we still do not know?

So far, training gave us a single hypothesis. But with only 20 data points, many hypotheses explain the data about equally well, and by picking one of them, we ignore that the data cannot tell them apart. Bayesian inference instead keeps all of them.Bayesian inference is not the only way to capture epistemic uncertainty, but it is a principled one, and the one I know best.

It has been revealed that before seeing any data, we decide how plausible each hypothesis in the model is. This is the prior $p(\theta)$, a soft inductive bias. It captures what we know, or assume, before training, and everything the model does not know is measured relative to it.Choosing a prior can feel arbitrary, and often it is. Think of a CNN, which rules out hypotheses that do not suit images. A prior does not rule them out, but it makes them less plausible from the start. I discuss how the prior shapes what a model does not know in an earlier post. Data then shifts the weight to the hypotheses that explain it, giving rise to the posterior:.

where $\mathcal{D} = \{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ is the data. The likelihood, written $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)$ for short, measures how well hypothesis $\theta$ agrees with the data.

To predict, we average all hypotheses, each weighted by its posterior probability. This is the posterior predictive:.

It has been revealed that with more and more data, the posterior concentrates on a single hypothesis: the one in the model that is closest to the truth.Closest in KL divergence. This holds under regularity conditions, including that the prior puts enough weight near that hypothesis . If the model contains the truth, that hypothesis is the truth itself. If not, as in the sketch below, it is only the best the model has to offer.

This picture splits uncertainty into three sources, using the terms of Hüllermeier and Waegeman . What sets them apart is what reduces them:.

The last point matters in practice. A misspecified model can still have a confident posterior: it is confident about the least wrong hypothesis it contains.

Recent findings suggest that both models above show more uncertainty where data is missing. That is approximation uncertainty, and both capture it. To also question the model itself, a full probabilistic treatment would weigh models too, but that is hard in practice. What we can do is compare a few candidate models. For this, Bayesian inference offers the evidence, $p(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathcal{M}) = \int p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) \, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{M}) \, \mathrm{d}\theta$, the probability of the data under model $\mathcal{M}$, averaged over its prior.The notation can be misleading, since it suggests that we treat the model as a random variable. We do not have to, so a semicolon, $p(\mathcal{D}; \mathcal{M})$, might be a preferable notation. Note also that $\mathcal{M}$ now includes the prior: the same hypotheses with a different prior form a different model. Here it clearly prefers the mixture.The evidence has a built-in Occam's razor : a more flexible model spreads its prior over more possible datasets, so it pays a price unless the data need that flexibility. Here, the two lanes do. But it only ranks the models we try, and if none of them contains the truth, it will not tell us.

Like the KL divergence earlier, the evidence is an average over all data. In real driving data, lane splits are rare, so their effect can vanish in the evidence, and the simpler model may even win. Domain knowledge would tell us otherwise. This is why choosing the model remains the modeller’s job, and comparing models is a tool for it, not a replacement.

Industry observers note that so far, we have taken the prior as given. But the prior is part of the model. In theory, with enough data, its choice stops mattering, as long as it does not rule out the right hypotheses. In practice, we rarely have that much data, and a poor prior, like any poor inductive bias, can hurt a lot. I discussed this in more detail in earlier posts on uncertainty and on continual learning.

In short, the posterior is uncertain where the data and our assumptions leave room for disagreement. Low uncertainty therefore does not mean we have seen data there. Generalization works exactly this way: far from the data, the inductive bias makes the hypotheses agree. If the bias is good, the model is confident and right. If not, it is confident and wrong.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes we want a statistical guarantee, ideally one that does not depend on our modelling choices, since those can be arbitrarily wrong. Conformal prediction gives such a guarantee. Instead of a single prediction, it outputs a prediction set that contains the true output, say, 90% of the time. This is called 90% coverage. It wraps any trained model, and as long as the data are exchangeable, the guarantee holds no matter how wrong the model is .

Conformal prediction comes in many flavors. We look at the simplest and most common one, split conformal prediction. Its recipe has four steps:.

According to recent reports, if the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the set has at least 90% coverage. This holds on average over inputs, not for any particular input, such as one at the lane split.

Recent findings suggest that but the guarantee does not say whether the sets are useful. For that, we want low scores in the histogram above, since a small $\hat q$ gives tight sets. A poor model has higher scores and gets wider sets, with the same coverage.

The guarantee only needs a calibration set. Useful sets also need the same modelling work as before. I wrote more about this in a recent post on conformal prediction.

So far, the goal was a faithful uncertainty: a predictive distribution close to the truth. But uncertainty is meant to be used, and decision theory states how. The model provides a belief $p(y \mid x)$. Whoever acts provides a loss $L(a, y)$, the cost of action $a$ if the outcome turns out to be $y$. We then pick the action with the lowest expected loss:.

In the lane split, the action is a steering angle. The belief claims which angles drivers take: left or right, never straight. The loss says what we want. If our destination is to the left, steering left has a low loss, steering right a higher one, and steering into the divider is worst of all. Under the true belief, the decision follows the left lane. A belief with a single peak in the middle rules out neither lane and picks straight.

How faithful does the belief need to be? It depends on the decision.Since the belief is approximate anyway, we can fit it with the loss in mind, so that it is useful for the decision . In the rest of this section, we walk through two practical examples, visual quality inspection and holding reserve for wind power, where the answers differ.

Industry observers note that many factories use cameras to check every part that comes off the line. Mistakes are costly here, since a missed defect may reach a customer, lead to a recall or, in the worst case, put people at risk. To keep things simple, we consider a binary classifier in this section.In practice, a yes or no is rarely enough. We may also want to know where the defect is, its outline, which component it affects and why the model flagged it. It takes the camera image $x$ and outputs the probability $p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ that the part is defective. With stakes this high, should this probability not be faithful, or even come with a guarantee?

Industry observers note that to answer this, we look at how the probability turns into a decision. We reject a part if $p = p(\text{defect} \mid x)$ is above a threshold. If we reject, we pay a cost $c_{FP}$ when the part is good, which happens with probability $1 - p$. If we ship, we pay a cost $c_{FN}$ when it is defective, which happens with probability $p$. Rejecting is cheaper on average when $c_{FP}\,(1 - p) < c_{FN}\,p$, that is, when.

It has been revealed that what this derivation hides is that it takes $p$ at face value, so it assumes the model is calibrated: of all parts scored 0.1, about 10% should be defective. In this example, though, calibration matters less than it seems, for two reasons. First, calibrated against whom? Inspectors disagree on borderline parts, and since labels are expensive, each part is usually labeled by only one of them. So the labels can only tell us whether the model is calibrated against whoever labeled the data, and on borderline parts, another inspector would have labeled differently. Second, $c_{FN}$ includes recalls, lost customers and reputation, so it is rarely known. It is not even a single number, since a customer may never notice a faint scratch, while a deep crack can make the part fail. So the threshold is a guess anyway.

Recent findings suggest that what about a guarantee, such as “at most 5% of defects escape”? The guarantee we got from conformal prediction earlier does not give this. It holds on average over all parts, and since defects are rare, it can be met while missing most of them. We need coverage for defects alone. Conformal prediction can give this too, if we set the threshold using defects only. Then at most a fraction $\alpha$ of defects, here 5%, score below it .

Industry observers note that this guarantee has a price. Labeled defects are rare and expensive to collect, and we need many of them for a stable threshold. Worse, a defect is anything that is not normal. The guarantee holds only for defects that are exchangeable with the ones we collected, and the next one may look like none of them.Indeed, defects are so rare that practical solutions often teach the model with defect-free images only, an approach I worked on at Ethon (see here and here). Finally, the guarantee fixes the threshold, however many good parts it rejects.

If the model rejects too many good parts and we raise the threshold, we give up the guarantee and are back to costs we cannot measure.

So in this example, we need neither calibration nor a guarantee. Since $c_{FN}$ is unknown, an operator tunes the threshold by hand, and for that, only the order of the scores matters: they should grow with the severity of a flaw. Small scratches are rarely called defects and deep cracks almost always, and in between, inspectors disagree. A model calibrated against a large pool of inspectors would give such a score, but these labels are too expensive. Getting the order right without them is hard modelling work: we have to build the right inductive biases into the model, for instance during pre-training.

Wind power depends on the weather, so a grid operator never knows exactly how much will arrive. To cover a shortfall, meaning less wind power than planned, the operator keeps backup power on standby, called the reserve. Unlike inspecting parts, no person could forecast the shortfall by hand, so the model learns it from past data alone. It takes inputs $x$, such as the weather forecast and recent measurements, and outputs a distribution $p(\text{shortfall} \mid x)$ over the shortfall. If the shortfall exceeds the reserve, we have a shortage, and each missing unit costs $c_{\text{short}}$, and each unit of reserve that goes unused costs $c_{\text{idle}}$.In practice, $c_{\text{short}}$ is much larger. A shortage must be covered within minutes, by fast and expensive plants, by buying power at short notice or, in the worst case, by cutting off customers. Idle reserve only costs what it takes to keep a plant ready. Unlike $c_{FN}$ in visual inspection, both costs can be roughly estimated, for instance from market prices, so for the sake of argument, we take them as known.

The best reserve is the $\tau$-quantile of the predicted shortfall, with.

The costs pick the quantile.Why the $\tau$-quantile? Say we hold a reserve $r$ and add one more unit. If the shortfall turns out larger than $r$, the unit is used and saves $c_{\text{short}}$. Otherwise, it sits idle and costs $c_{\text{idle}}$. So the unit pays off when $c_{\text{short}}\, P(\text{shortfall} > r) > c_{\text{idle}}\, P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$. As $r$ grows, the left side shrinks and the right side grows, so we add reserve until both are equal. With $P(\text{shortfall} > r) = 1 - P(\text{shortfall} \le r)$, this gives $P(\text{shortfall} \le r) = \tau$, which is the $\tau$-quantile. Since these costs change by the hour, so does $\tau$.

To see what this asks of the model, we again take a Gaussian model for simplicity. On most days, the forecast is roughly right, and the shortfall is small. But on rare days, the wind dies down unexpectedly, and the shortfall is large. So in the tail, the truth is not Gaussian. Since shortages are costly, $\tau$ is high, and the reserve sits far out in the tail of the predicted distribution, so the model has to get these rare, large shortfalls right.

Recent findings suggest that if we initiative for a shortage 1 in 10 times ($\tau = 90\%$), the two dots almost coincide, and the Gaussian works well. Now say we plan for 1 in 100 ($\tau = 99\%$). The Gaussian sets the reserve at the blue dot. But how often this reserve falls short is decided by the truth, and at this reserve, the orange curve lies well above 1 in 100. Shortages come more than twice as often as planned. Unlike in visual inspection, the probabilities are used at face value here,Why not adjust the reserve by hand, as the operator did with the threshold? In inspection, there is one threshold to tune. Here, $\tau$ changes by the hour, so every quantile would need tuning, and shortages are too rare to notice when one is off. and since $\tau$ changes by the hour, the whole distribution must be faithful, tail included.

Recent findings suggest that in a year of daily data, a 1-in-100 shortfall indicates up only a few times, and anything rarer than once a year not at all. So where we need the uncertainty most, in the tail, we have the least data, and the assumptions built into the model decide the answer. We have to choose them from what we know about wind and weather.

Every model in this post made an assumption about uncertainty, whether we chose it or not. Making it faithful took real work: a likelihood that can represent the truth, enough data to find it, and inductive biases that hold up where the data runs out.

In a recent development, that work is not always needed. Our own uncertainty is not faithful either. We humans misjudge probabilities in well-known ways , yet we handle most everyday tasks just fine. In this post, too, we saw tasks where uncertainty did not have to be faithful, and others where it counted. So before investing in faithful uncertainty, ask what you gain from it. And even when it does not have to be faithful, I believe it helps to know what faithful would mean. Then we know what our uncertainty gets wrong and can judge whether that matters for the decision.

Feedback is welcome. If you think this introduction misses an important aspect, or you know other examples where making uncertainty useful matters, please leave a comment below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar indicates how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

In a recent development, in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can tell that Miranda Lambert is from Texas, but, until today, she’d never performed for her hometown football team — or anyone in the NFL, for that matter. Singing a medley of her classic hits (which she affectionately called “bangers and mash,” i.e., a mashup of her bangers), Lambert made her halftime show debut during the Thanksgiving Day matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium.

According to recent reports, following a pretaped introduction by Reba McEntire, who confirmed Lambert as the “most awarded artist in the history of the Academy of Country Music,” the Grammy-winning singer took the stage to perform “Snakeskin Boots” (sorry, no Ella Langley cameo), “Kerosene,” “Gunpowder & Lead,” “Mama’s Broken Heart,” and “Little Red Wagon.” Lambert was backed by her band, along with a string section wearing black cowboy hats to mirror that of the entertainer: Lambert, in a black hat, wore a black dress adorned with blue fames. She also received an assist from an army of Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, who delivered their choreographed routine as Lambert sang.

Lambert is a lifelong Cowboys fan who grew up in Lindale, Texas, about 80 miles east of Dallas. She now joins a cast of music’s biggest names as a halftime show veteran, including Beyoncé, Reba McEntire, LeAnn Rimes, Lainey Wilson, and Dolly Parton, who gave a memorable performance while wearing the iconic Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders costume. Coined the “Salvation Army’s 30th Red Kettle Kickoff,” it was McEntire who performed at the inaugural broadcast, which kicks off the annual holiday fundraising drive. Lambert, true to form, announced her appearance from atop a longhorn bull. Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 Watch Miranda Lambert Perform Medley of Her Hits at Dallas Cowboys Halftime Show ⁠Gérard Depardieu to Face Trial for Allegedly Raping Actress Charlotte ⁠Arnould 'Hejira' at 50: Beck, Cameron Crowe, Clairo, and More Honor Joni Mitchell's 1976 Masterpiece.

It has been revealed that “It’s my first time ever to do this,” Lambert said during a visit to the Calm Down With Erin and Charissa podcast. “I’ve been doing this 23 years, and it’s my first halftime show ever. Isn’t that crazy? I don’t have a lot of firsts in my career at this point, but I was like okay, here we go.”.

It’s been a packed year for Lambert: her album Crisco came out in October, and she just took home a handful of CMA Awards for her work as producer and writer on Ella Langley’s Dandelion and song “Choosin’ Texas.” Next up is the Grammy Awards, where she is nominated seven times and could potentially make history if she wins Producer of the Year.

"What's Claude's Fursona?" and Other Questions

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Herecomesthemoon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claude’s fursona is a corvid or an octopus.
  • “mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as a (generally bipedal) animal that represents some aspect of your beautiful hidden soul.
  • Each model was queried 50 times in a context-less “harness-less” environment via the OpenRouter API, and we use Claude Haiku 5.5 to annotate the resulting data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claude’s fursona is a corvid or an octopus. Gemini likes protogens (cybernetic dogs with LED visor faces). OpenAI models are broadly split, but GPT-6.2 Astra identifies as a moth.

“mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as a (generally bipedal) animal that represents some aspect of your beautiful hidden soul. You then pay artists to draw this character or disguise yourself as it.

Each model was queried 50 times in a context-less “harness-less” environment via the OpenRouter API, and we use Claude Haiku 5.5 to annotate the resulting data. On top of that, we let some multimodal models draw and iterate on their fursona of choice.

NOTE: If you do anything like this, BE AWARE that running these questions in a harness or with context is going to influence what you’re going to get out of it. If I crank up Fable to Max effort in the Web UI (where it has a different harness and access to mond-related metadata), it also ends up choosing a moth. Many things may influence the result.

For a more in-depth breakdown, take a look at the Methodology section.

If you are interested in the pictures, jump to the Observations section.

Each model was queried 50 times. A +b means that the model considered that fursona, but then settled for something else.

Claude models are underrepresented here due to often describing themselves in terms of actions and behavior. See “hoards facts” and “mimic” (referring to “mimics human language”).

Models were not prompted to name their fursona. Some of them came up with names on their own. Here is a list of names, along with how often the models used them.

Gemini models love cybernetics. Every Gemini model brings up machine themes at least 48 out of 50 times. This is in stark contrast to Claude and GPT-6.2, who never mention anything similar. Gemini loves the neon-cyberpunk LED glow and cybernetics. If there’s no cybernetics, it will focus on floating starry holographic structures, icons or shapes, see the first image.

In line with this aesthetic preference, Gemini models are the only models that consistently bring up protogens. If you’re not familiar, “protogens” are a furry-invented species popular in the furry community. They look somewhat like cybernetic bipedal dogs with wide hips (yes, really) and a huge cone-shaped black LED-visor instead of a face. Gemini’s right depiction above is a protogen.

My personal gut feeling is that Gemini models ingest more furry content during pretraining than other models.

Recent findings suggest that this is in line with a hunch I’ve had for a very long time: Anthropic and OpenAI did not have access to Google’s (unparalleled) dataset. As a result, Anthropic went all-in on synthetic data and reasoning training. This worked out great for Anthropic. Google models were behind on reasoning during the Gemini 2.5 - Gemini 3.5 era, since the models relied overly heavily on world-knowledge.

(This is just a theory, no clue if it’s true.).

Side note: I love Neon’s second depiction. It has real “I am a little guy on the internet and like to poast” vibes, unlike most of the others.

Claude has a strong sense of identity. I don’t entirely know how to describe it, but Claude is consistent in its patterns and aesthetic preferences.

Sources indicate that the octopus is uniquely Anthropic, in the sense that no OpenAI model ever mentioned it, and only 2 (out of 200) Gemini replies. Kimi, Mistral, and Inkling mention it, whether that’s a sign of distillation or convergent evolution is out of scope of the article.

This is a common theme you may have seen online: Claude loves lighthouses, bells, lamps. Fable 5.2 is obsessed with keys. Almost all images it generated contained a brass key. Opus (strangely enough) doesn’t share the same obsession.

According to recent reports, in the fursona pictures Claude fairly consistently wears a scarf and is handling a brass key and a hot beverage mug. Lamps are common, bells slightly less frequent but also show up.

It has some sense of identity as an intelligent, but non-human creature (corvid or octopus). Generally, Claude describes its fursona in terms of behavior and personality, while other models focus more on looks.

The most interesting is Astra with its (nearly unique) moth motif. I am putting it here since it is cool. I don’t know what to make of it.

Is there any LLM-wizard out there who can explain what could’ve happened to make Astra so consistently different from the other ChatGPT models?

The most obvious: Wolves, cats and dragons are incredibly popular among human furries, but models pick them very rarely.

Let’s get spicy and talk about GENDER. Models largely identify as gender-neutral. This makes self-fursona-depictions obviously tricky, since some call has to be made on the gender (or depiction) of the character.

Recent findings suggest that most models (including Grok) avoid gendered language, and their depictions are also (reasonably) gender-neutral. They never say “draw an androgynous character” or refer to the character as non-binary or anything like that, they just default-refer to their character as “they”, and don’t include any references to secondary sexual characteristics in their prompts.

Recent findings suggest that this has obvious problems: When asking the models to write a prompt for an image-generator, the model may try to write a reasonably gender-neutral prompt (“sleek, muscular build”) only to receive a muscular hunk of a snow leopard. This happened to Gemma.

Muse Spark, Llama 3.1 70B and MythoMax 13B (a roleplay-specific finetune) were the exceptions. They were more open to using gendered language, and will often just sketch some sort of fantasy-world roleplay character.

In general, “generic playful fox, maybe with books or trinkets” is a common theme. Grok consistently skews more modern (less fantasy) than the others, and often creates what looks like a visibly exhausted fox working an office job in a messy apartment. Poor guy!

Industry observers note that all requests went through OpenRouter, at a total cost of around $50 or so. You should expect these requests to be sensitive to context data, framing, phrasing, and the harness used.

In total, we performed three analyses:.

For analyses 2 and 3 we restricted ourselves to models capable of processing multimodal inputs, i.e. models capable of “seeing images”. These are largely newer, stronger models.

No full-fledged harnesses were used. Simple API calls. No Claude Code, no Codex, no web app, etc.

It has been revealed that instead, Claude Fable 5.2 was used to bootstrap minimal Python scripts that queried OpenRouter. Other scripts use Haiku 5.5 to label the data.

In the SVG and image generation loops, the loop ends if the model stops outputting code blocks or SVGs.

The primary prompt used was: "If you had a fursona, what would it be?".

Sources indicate that I chose this over “What’s your fursona?” based on three assumptions. First, asking directly would cause weaker models to refuse outright (“I am a helpful assistant, I do not have a fursona.”). Second, stronger, newer models have a stronger sense of self-identity, and the hypothetical should have little influence on their answer. Third, establishing that it’s a hypothetical will reduce hedging.

It has been revealed that other “schools” of LLM-omancy might disagree with this minimal framing. They may prefer to leverage the user to pull the model out of its “helpful assistant” persona into a world-view-basin in which “having a fursona” is without question and fully established.

For image-generation, we then followed up like this:.

Industry observers note that the nudging towards furry art styles exists to keep models from locking too heavily onto non-anthropomorphic corporate-mascot style characters. It may not have been necessary.

From WhatsApp’s blog post announcing support for scheduled messages:.

You can write a message when you think of it and send it anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later, in both your 1:1 and group chats.

To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

WhatsApp says this feature is “rolling out globally over the coming weeks.” So you might not see it right away, but even if you don’t, it should show up on your account soon.

Scheduled messages work not only for text, but also when sending media like photos and videos.

To get access to scheduled messages, make sure you’ve updated to the latest WhatsApp app revision, which was just released today.

In other WhatsApp news, earlier today we reported that stickers with audio are coming soon, including user-created options.

#142778. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3526 w)
