Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Industry observers note that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Industry observers note that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

In a recent development, the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that the screen demonstrates my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics organization. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

It has been revealed that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” notes Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

It has been revealed that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

According to recent reports, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

According to recent reports, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Industry observers note that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Industry observers note that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga states, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just substantial enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Newly introduced York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

It has been revealed that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics tech giant XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” indicates Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Recent findings suggest that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson indicates. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Industry observers note that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

In a recent development, but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more key than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell indicates. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu states.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Recent findings suggest that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra states, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Recent findings suggest that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

In a recent development, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Recent findings suggest that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Sources indicate that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sources indicate that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

It has been revealed that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga states they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this newly introduced technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that according to a upcoming Counterpoint Research report, Apple increased its share of Latin America’s smartphone shipments in Q3 2026, recording the smallest decline among the region’s top five brands. Here are the details.

In a report released this week, Counterpoint Research says the ongoing memory crunch led to a 24% year-over-year drop in smartphone shipments during Q3, “the second-lowest quarter since 2015.”.

In a recent development, per the report, Samsung maintained its lead with a 35% shipment share, despite a 15% year-over-year decline in total shipments, well ahead of second-place Motorola, which captured 18% of shipments after a 23% drop. Interestingly, Motorola’s share actually increased one percentage point from a year earlier.

Rounding out the top five were Xiaomi, with a 14% share and a whopping 34% decline, Apple, with a 9% share and a 10% decline, and Honor, with an 8% share and a 27% decline.

Despite the decline in overall shipments, Apple’s shipment share increased by 2 percentage points from 7% a year earlier, moving the company from fifth to fourth place in the region.

Other brands collectively accounted for 16% of shipments, down from 19% a year earlier, with their combined shipments falling 37% year over year.

Here’s Counterpoint on Apple’s performance for Q3 in Latin America:.

Sources indicate that apple was the most resilient, with the smallest decline among the top five brands (shipments down 10% YoY), and rose one position to No. 4 in the region. Apple absorbed the impact of price increases better than its rivals, helped by strong product availability. Apple debuted the iPhone 18 Pro series at the end of the quarter. For the first time, Chile joined Brazil and Mexico in the first launch wave.

As for regional factors that contributed to the decline, Senior Analyst Benjamin Corona noted that Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia faced additional challenges beyond the global memory shortage, ranging from political uncertainty to inflation and tighter household budgets. Smartphone shipments fell 22%, 26%, and 28% in those countries, respectively.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint says it “expects the decline to ease in Q4 2026 as prices stabilize and seasonal demand returns,” adding that “memory-related price pressure should moderate by Q2 2027, but supply constraints will likely continue through the end of 2027.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the release of the prequel The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, franchise producer Nina Jacobson regrets splitting the Mockingjay films into two parts.

At the time, The Twilight Saga and Harry Potter split their grand finale into two films, and Lionsgate followed suit, breaking up the last Suzanne Collins book of the OG Hunger Games trilogy into two films as well.

“Even though I love the Mockingjay films, if I had it to do over again, I think both Francis [Lawrence, director] and I might try to do it all in one,” she said in an interview with Empire.

Sources indicate that she continued, “Mockingjay was such a substantial book, and it takes you to so many different places. But in the end, I think that Francis and I both felt that splitting them up… even if it did come from an inside-out place of really feeling like we needed two films to tell the story, I think audiences find it cynical. Even if its intentions are earnest, which they were. They feel like it’s a play to make them see two films instead of one.” Watch on Deadline.

With Collins’ two prequels like The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes and Sunrise on the Reaping, producers have changed the way they adapt the books.

In a recent development, “We really put the burden on ourselves [now], even when it’s a big book, to transform it into a theatrical experience, to not take advantage of your audience’s patience, to make it as tight as we can,” Jacobson told the publication. “[Sunrise On The Reaping] is the longest by a minute or two of all of them.”.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping sees Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson return to their roles from the original trilogy. The film stars Joseph Zada playing a young Haymitch, and is joined by Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Glenn Close (Drusilla), Ralph Finneas (President Snow), Billy Porter (Magno), Maya Hawke (Wiress), Elle Fanning (Effie), Percy Daggs IV (Ampert), Whitney Peak (Lenore Dove), Lili Taylor (Mags), Kiran Culkin (Caesar Flickerman), Kelvin Harrison Jr (Beetee), Jesse Plemons (Plutarch), Ben Wang (Wyatt), among others.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.
  • It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.
  • In a recent development, identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

In a recent development, identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

According to recent reports, intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

Sources indicate that we recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:.

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:.

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:.

According to recent reports, if you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

It has been revealed that after editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Industry observers note that note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare latest interpolations to the existing instance sources and update them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

It has been revealed that for TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open complications and we will try to accomodate them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Sources indicate that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving leftovers are officially on the menu, Black Friday deals are calling, and the long holiday weekend is practically begging for a marathon TV session. The best latest movies and shows to watch this weekend serve up a delicious buffet of suburban scandal, futuristic sci-fi and workplace hijinks. There's also one of the biggest documentaries of all time, a football-fueled war drama and a family-friendly adventure starring Chris Pratt.

As Tom's Guide's streaming editor, I've rounded up and ranked this week's biggest releases to help you decide what's worth your precious downtime. A scandalous group of wealthy hunting-happy housewives returns with more secrets to spill, a beloved sci-fi universe gets a fresh spin and Amy Poehler reunites with "Parks and Recreation" co-creator Michael Schur. On the movie front, there's a documentary that will mess with your head, a World War II story that brings football onto the battlefield, and a feel-good coming-of-age drama with a Navy SEAL twist.

So after you grab all those Black Friday streaming deals and claim your spot on the couch, here's what to watch this weekend, ranked by must-watch factor.

Kelly recently reviewed "Black Doves" season 2 and "The Gilded Age" season 4.

Industry observers note that genre: DocumentaryRuntime: 2 hrs 54 minWhat it's about: What happens when one of America's most infamous fraudsters invites a camera crew into her home? Nathan Fielder ("The Rehearsal") and Lance Oppenheim get startlingly close to Elizabeth Holmes in the 34 days before she reports to prison for the Theranos scandal. With partner Billy Evans also in the mix, what begins as an intimate portrait of a disgraced entrepreneur rapidly takes some very unexpected turns.Why you should watch: This is no conventional true-crime documentary, but a gloriously strange, frequently hilarious and increasingly unsettling experiment in reality, performance and the slippery business of telling the truth. Fielder's trademark deadpan questioning makes for some jaw-dropping exchanges, but the less you know about where this nearly three-hour ride is headed, the better. Where to watch: Prime Video (with purchase).

Sources indicate that genre: Soapy dramaAvailable now: All 8 episodes (about 50 min each)What it's about: Maple Brook's most scandalous residents are back, and the body count isn't going down. Months after season 1's deadly finale, Sophie (Brittany Snow) and Margo (Malin Åkerman) are on the outs. But old secrets, new enemies and another murder investigation bring the dangerously codependent duo back together. Meanwhile, Margo's husband is making a play for the Texas governor's mansion.Why you should watch: Think "Desperate Housewives" with more guns and girl-on-girl tension. The second season promises another helping of steamy entanglements. If you thought these ladies couldn't possibly make things messier, bless your heart.Where to watch: Netflix.

Industry observers note that genre: War dramaRuntime: 2 hrs 7 minWhat it's about: After Pearl Harbor, four standout college football players enlist in the Marines and head into the Pacific theater. As they face the horrors of combat, the young men (Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis) get one last chance to take the field together in the legendary Mosquito Bowl, a football game held on Christmas Eve 1944 ahead of the Battle of Okinawa.Why you should watch: Director Peter Berg reunites with sports storyteller Buzz Bissinger, who made “Friday Night Lights” a classic, but this time the stakes are considerably more brutal. The football sequences deliver plenty of adrenaline, while the harrowing battle scenes make this a sobering reminder of the human cost of war. Where to watch: Netflix.

According to recent reports, genre: Sci-fi dramaAvailable now: All 8 episodes (about 1 hour each)What it's about: It's 2099, and Los Angeles has a fresh ruling class: our robot overlords. Following an uprising, Replicants have taken control. Human fugitive Cora (Hunter Schafer) assumes the identity of a Blade Runner and gets paired with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Replicant nearing the end of her life. Their mission? Sources indicate that genre: Romantic fantasy comedy-dramaRuntime: 1 hr 45 minWhat it's about: Tired of being mocked by her seaside village, a fiercely independent Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) decides to commission herself a husband made entirely of wicker. Her unconventional marriage to the remarkably devoted creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sends the conservative townsfolk into a tizzy.Why you should watch: Colman and Skarsgård have unexpectedly lovely chemistry in this offbeat romantic fairytale, which mixes saucy humor and social rebellion. The playful take on marriage, female independence and what makes a good husband is as funny as it is surprisingly heartfelt. Where to watch: Prime Video (with purchase).

According to recent reports, mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla free access to models that are finding more complex bugs.

Mozilla’s Firefox team now spends 27% of its effort fixing security flaws, up from about 10% a year ago, Firefox head Ajit Varma told Business Insider. The rise comes as AI models find more bugs in the browser.

Varma mentioned OpenAI and Anthropic give Mozilla, a nonprofit, “a lot of tokens for free”. Their models, he said, “are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser.”.

In April, Mozilla patched 271 Firefox bugs found by Anthropic’s Mythos. OpenAI’s newly introduced GPT-6 Cyber model has since turned up 81 more. Rival browsers face the same surge: Chrome patched a record 429 bugs in June.

According to recent reports, varma still thinks the pace of AI gives his team “enough time” to fix problems before the next leap. He is also using AI to make Firefox faster and stop memory leaks.

“There’s a lot of routine activities that we don’t necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it’s relentless; it doesn’t get tired,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that others are less relaxed. Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned last week that AI-found bugs mean more outages, as companies rush out fixes faster than they can test them.

Industry News: I did slow-motion strength training for a week — my muscles have never worked this hard, and I noticed some surprising benefits

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when I head to the gym, I have a bad habit of wanting to get in and get back out, which means I can rush through sessions without really thinking about what I'm doing.
  • With that in mind, I decided to slow things down for a week and try "slow-motion strength training," which means slowing down reps of your exercises.
  • Industry observers note that it feels more challenging, and it's harder to control your reps, which means your form has to be on point if you want to work the muscles properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when I head to the gym, I have a bad habit of wanting to get in and get back out, which means I can rush through sessions without really thinking about what I'm doing. Plus, I've been a trainer for a while now, too, so it does feel like I'm on autopilot sometimes.

With that in mind, I decided to slow things down for a week and try "slow-motion strength training," which means slowing down reps of your exercises. It can also be referred to as time under tension, which means your muscles spend longer contracting, and you naturally increase volume without lifting heavier.

Industry observers note that it feels more challenging, and it's harder to control your reps, which means your form has to be on point if you want to work the muscles properly. Below, I explain the TUT technique in more detail, plus I tell you about the surprising benefits I noticed from a week of slowing it down.

TUT uses tempo to make your muscles work harder without changing the amount of resistance. This way, you can extend the total time worked. There are typically four stages — the concentric phase (when muscles shorten or contract), the eccentric phase (when the muscle lengthens), and the pauses between them every rep.

For example, a squat programmed at a 4-1-4-1 tempo would mean lifting the weight for four seconds (concentric loading), pausing for one second, then lowering the weight (eccentric loading) for four seconds, followed by a pause at the end of the rep. Adding a longer pause adopts an isometric contraction — placing muscle under stress without shortening or lengthening.

Recent findings suggest that time under tension is predominantly found in weightlifting, but not exclusively. The idea is that you'll improve endurance, but also hypertrophy, which is the process of building muscle; more challenge during an exercise could help build muscle without lifting heavier weights.

It's thought that the eccentric focus can actually build muscle, stability and control. Eccentric movement is where the muscle lengthens while under tension, and it's actively resisting a force whilst being stretched, and it helps you build control rather than just dropping the weight down.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This can create more muscle damage, leading to greater growth and adaptation during recovery. It's also beneficial for flexibility, joint stability and injury prevention. That noted, concentric rep phases are still crucial for building muscle strength, improving power and training muscles to exert force.

When a controlled "injury" to muscle fibers happens during exercise, your body begins its healing process during rest and produces growth hormone, which is vital for muscle adaptation. It’s how you build muscle — you break it down to build it up stronger — a process called hypertrophy.

A slower tempo will still primarily recruit the slow-twitch muscle fibers (or sometimes a mix of both), which are responsible for longer workout efforts, improving endurance.

According to recent reports, crucially, though, we know that a strong indicator of adaptation is how close to failure and how much output you put into your reps and sets. Could slowing things down improve that for me?

I decided to adopt a 4-1-4-1 tempo for 6-8 reps of each exercise. In my upper-body workout, I chose the bench press, triceps dips, barbell rows and pull-ups, with any accessory work remaining at normal tempo. Then, for lower-body, I opted for a barbell RDL, barbell squats, Bulgarian split squats and bench hip thrusts. Again, any accessory work remained at a normal tempo, as I wanted to put the majority of my focus on my "massive lifts." This also meant the larger, more powerful muscle groups were holding tension for longer, allowing me to control the movements.

It has been revealed that the first thing I noticed was that I had to control my reps even more than normal, and what usually felt like the correct weight choice suddenly felt much harder. This was particularly true of the concentric phases, such as standing from a deadlift or squat, where I'm used to pushing upward with power pretty fast.

According to recent reports, I also supersetted my exercises, which means performing two exercises back-to-back; although this reduces your working time in the gym, it actually increases overall volume and reduces rest time. Coupled with slow-motion training, I felt absolutely wiped out after a week.

Sources indicate that I also noticed my DOMS (Delayed-Onset Muscle Soreness) far more than usual, and I was having to really dig in to complete the final reps. You ideally should be working this close to failure to achieve change in your muscles, but without your form slipping. I did have to reset a few times and go slightly lighter to keep my form in check, but I loved the increase in intensity, which meant I couldn't cruise like I might normally be tempted to do.

Time under tension techniques could help build muscle mass alongside progressive overload — adapting your routine incrementally as you get stronger. Other variables like rest, sleep, training frequency and protein matter an enormous amount, too, so try to get the basics in check before adding techniques like this to your routine.

In a recent development, I really enjoyed slowing it down for a week and feeling my muscles working hard. I felt fatigued all over after every session, and it helped me stay focused on all phases of the workout without rushing.

In a recent development, will I continue? Probably not, and I obviously didn't see physical changes in a week, but I might pepper more of this into my strength training from now on, even just to remind myself to slow down.

Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more.
  • Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct people to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the company responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the tech giant can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

In a recent development, apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:.

“The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed new (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”.

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”.

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s new restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its owners, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

According to recent reports, according to the tech giant, the incident began on November 19, when it started investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The tech giant noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:.

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our customers,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:.

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That mentioned, the firm confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The company also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Recent findings suggest that finally, 1Password remarked consumers do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York.
  • State-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft states.
  • In a recent development, the list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York.

State-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft states. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday.

In a recent development, the list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft notes state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.

“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.

The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies, as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record.

US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later stated Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks.

It has been revealed that crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported.

In a recent development, microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack. The new report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.

In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.

The attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft notes.

The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.

“ARTEX does not introduce latest attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.

Recent findings suggest that attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.

In a recent development, microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win shows the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.

#142756. Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount

Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lia

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture.
  • In a recent development, the results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page.
  • There is a better way to measure culture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the manufacturer as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.

In a recent development, the results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.

There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.

Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of consumers. That’s it.

The square root is key. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a organization of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.

We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient.

The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.

Sources indicate that to account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders. Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).

In a recent development, if P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.

Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.

For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com:.

Recent findings suggest that as with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the firm logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.

It is also worth monitoring the rate of change. A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip:, :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.

Industry observers note that if your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.

Industry observers note that if you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.

Sources indicate that culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

The charges stemmed from alleged incidents involving two minor boys on the New Mexico set of the Fox/Warner Bros TV series The Cleaning Lady. Busfield, who directed several episodes of Cleaning Lady during its four-season run from 2022-25, mentioned the claims were “absolutely one gazillion percent untrue. On this day, as we all acknowledge the blessings in our lives, we send our love and eternal gratitude to each and every one of you.” Watch on Deadline.

The charges were tossed last month after the “prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner, including the failure to properly instruct the grand jury on the law for calling witnesses and in instructing the grand jurors on a procedure that effectively withheld requested witnesses,” Judge Joseph Montano wrote in an order quashing the indictment. “In doing so, the grand jury proceedings were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system and the presumption of prejudice applies.”.

Montano gave prosecutors the option to “institute latest criminal proceedings” against Busfield; each count in the tossed indictment carried a maximum sentence of six years behind bars.
